artifacts.name: Apollo Lunar Module
artifacts.title: Apollo Lunar Module
artifacts.summary: The spacecraft descent stages that carried humanity's first explorers to the lunar surface and remain as permanent monuments across six landing sites on the Moon.
artifacts.subtitle: The octagonal gold-and-aluminized-Kapton descent stages served as both landing craft and launchpad for twelve Apollo astronauts across six historic lunar expeditions.
artifacts.discoveries: Enabled the collection of 382 kilograms of lunar rocks and core samples, proving that the Moon formed from a giant impact with early Earth over 4.5 billion years ago.
artifacts.ending: When each crew fired their ascent engine to return to lunar orbit, the heavy descent stage was intentionally left behind on the lunar regolith as a permanent launch platform.
artifacts.legacy: Each descent stage bears a stainless-steel commemorative plaque and remains preserved in the airless lunar vacuum — photographed from orbit by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter.

artifacts.name: Opportunity Rover
artifacts.title: Opportunity Rover
artifacts.summary: Designed for a 90-sol mission, Opportunity traversed 45 kilometers of Martian plains for nearly 15 years before a planet-encircling dust storm ended its signal.
artifacts.subtitle: Engineered for a 90-Martian-day warranty, the golf-cart-sized solar rover operated for 5,111 sols (nearly 15 Earth years) and completed the first extraterrestrial marathon.
artifacts.discoveries: Discovered spherical hematite "blueberries" and gypsum veins inside Endeavour Crater, providing conclusive geological proof that ancient Mars once hosted warm, neutral liquid water.
artifacts.ending: In June 2018, the most intense planet-encircling Martian dust storm in decades blotted out the Sun over Perseverance Valley, draining Opportunity’s solar batteries.
artifacts.legacy: Transformed Mars exploration from "Follow the Water" to "Seek Signs of Ancient Life," directly paving the path for Curiosity and Perseverance.

artifacts.name: Ingenuity Helicopter
artifacts.title: Ingenuity Helicopter
artifacts.summary: The first aircraft to achieve powered, controlled flight on another planet, completing 72 historic flights before a rotor blade strike grounded it forever in Valinor Hills.
artifacts.subtitle: Weighing just 1.8 kilograms on Earth, Ingenuity proved that powered, controlled aerodynamic flight is possible in Mars’s atmosphere — which is less than 1% as dense as Earth’s.
artifacts.discoveries: Planned for 5 technology-demonstration flights over 30 days, Ingenuity evolved into an aerial scout for the Perseverance rover, completing 72 flights and flying 17 kilometers.
artifacts.ending: During a steep landing on featureless sand ripples on Flight 72 (January 18, 2024), its carbon-fiber rotor blades struck the dune surface, ending its flying career.
artifacts.legacy: Even grounded, Ingenuity continues to collect surface weather telemetry in Jezero Crater and has inspired a new generation of multi-rotor aerial explorers for Mars and Titan.

artifacts.name: ALSEP Scientific Packages
artifacts.title: ALSEP Scientific Packages
artifacts.summary: Nuclear-powered geophysical stations deployed by Apollo astronauts that recorded moonquakes, solar wind, and internal lunar heat for eight years after humanity left.
artifacts.subtitle: Autonomous, radioisotope-powered scientific observatories deployed by hand on the Moon to monitor the lunar environment long after astronauts departed.
artifacts.discoveries: Detected over 12,000 seismic events (moonquakes and meteoroid impacts), measured the Moon’s tenuous exosphere, and mapped the thickness of the lunar crust and mantle.
artifacts.ending: After operating faithfully for up to eight years, ground controllers transmitted the final termination command on September 30, 1977 due to budget reallocations.
artifacts.legacy: Passive laser retroreflectors placed alongside the packages still reflect laser pulses fired from Earth observatories today, measuring the Moon’s 3.8 cm annual drift.

artifacts.name: Surveyor 3
artifacts.title: Surveyor 3 Lander
artifacts.summary: The robotic scout that proved the lunar soil could support Apollo — and the only spacecraft ever visited on another world by human astronauts two years later.
artifacts.subtitle: A robotic triple-legged lunar lander equipped with a mechanical soil scoop and television camera that transmitted 6,315 images from inside a gentle lunar crater.
artifacts.discoveries: Confirmed that the lunar regolith was firm enough to bear the weight of a crewed Apollo Lunar Module rather than swallowing spacecraft in deep dust.
artifacts.ending: Fell silent after experiencing the extreme -150°C cold of its first two-week lunar night in May 1967.
artifacts.legacy: In November 1969, Apollo 12 astronauts Pete Conrad and Alan Bean landed just 180 meters away and walked over to inspect Surveyor 3 — the only time humans have visited a probe on another world.

artifacts.name: InSight Lander
artifacts.title: InSight Lander
artifacts.summary: A stationary planetary geofinder that listened to the heartbeat of Mars, detecting over 1,300 marsquakes and mapping the planet's liquid core before dust silenced its solar panels.
artifacts.subtitle: The first mission dedicated to peering deep beneath the Martian surface, deploying an ultra-sensitive dome-shielded seismometer directly onto the plains of Elysium Planitia.
artifacts.discoveries: Recorded 1,319 marsquakes — including a magnitude 4.7 tremor — allowing scientists to measure the depth of the Martian crust, mantle, and 1,830-km-radius liquid metal core.
artifacts.ending: Four years of fine red Martian dust coated its twin circular solar arrays until it could no longer recharge its batteries, sending a poignant final selfie in December 2022.
artifacts.legacy: Provided the first complete 3D interior map of another terrestrial planet beyond the Earth-Moon system.
